answer.summary: Ben Horowitz defines managerial leverage as the CEO getting more from an executive than they could by managing the team themselves: the executive—not the CEO—should identify what their department should do and how to advance the company. If the CEO has to keep prompting them, that leverage is absent.

sections.heading: What managerial leverage means
sections.content: A CEO has leverage when a leader independently tells the CEO what their department should do next and how they can move the company forward. The executive’s contribution lets the CEO accomplish more than if that person were not there; otherwise, the CEO could simply manage the team directly.

sections.heading: How to recognize when it is missing
sections.content: If the CEO has to repeatedly ask, “Why aren’t we doing this?” or “Why aren’t we doing that?”, Horowitz says the CEO is not getting leverage and should make a change. He contrasts this with a CEO’s role more broadly: the CEO need not generate every idea or give every order, but should gather and prioritize good ideas and align people around them.
